Lecture 16

Noncompact Haar Measure and the Modular Function

Lecture 5 integrated over compact groups. This lecture drops compactness. It asks which translation-invariant integrals a Lie group carries and how left and right integration differ. A noncompact Lie group has infinite Haar volume, so the normalised averaging of Lecture 5 is no longer available in general. Every Lie group has a left-invariant and a right-invariant density. With equal normalisations at the identity, the left density divided by the right density is the modular function. It controls right translation, inversion and the right regular representation.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Construct the left and right Haar densities of a Lie group, prove that each is unique up to a positive factor, and prove that the total mass is infinite when the group is noncompact.
  • Prove the right-translation and inversion identities for Δ(g)=∣det⁡Ad⁡(g)∣−1\Delta(g)=|\det\Ad(g)|^{-1}Δ(g)=∣detAd(g)∣−1.
  • Compute both Haar densities and Δ\DeltaΔ for the affine group ax+bax+bax+b.
  • Construct the left and right regular representations as strongly continuous unitary representations on L2(G)L^2(G)L2(G), and state the integration rules of Part II with their hypotheses.

Lecture 5 built a left-invariant density on a compact Lie group by translating a density at eee. That construction did not use compactness. Compactness entered later. It made the integral finite on every continuous function, and it allowed normalisation to total mass 111. It made the image of j(h)=∣det⁡Ad⁡(h)∣j(h)=|\det\Ad(h)|j(h)=∣detAd(h)∣ a compact subgroup of (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), so j≡1j\equiv1j≡1. It gave strict positivity through a finite cover. Without compactness we integrate only compactly supported functions. Strict positivity comes from charts, and jjj survives as a homomorphism. The left Haar density μL\mu_LμL​ below is the density δ\deltaδ of Lecture 5, and the modular function below is Δ=j−1\Delta=j^{-1}Δ=j−1.

Throughout, GGG is a Lie group of dimension nnn with Lie algebra g=TeG\g=T_eGg=Te​G. We write left translation, right translation, conjugation and inversion as Lg(x)=gx,Rg(x)=xg,Cg=Lg∘Rg−1,ι(x)=x−1.L_g(x)=gx,\qquad R_g(x)=xg,\qquad C_g=L_g\circ R_{g^{-1}},\qquad \iota(x)=x^{-1}.Lg​(x)=gx,Rg​(x)=xg,Cg​=Lg​∘Rg−1​,ι(x)=x−1. That gives gm=gks′s−1∈gkSS−1g_m=g_ks's^{-1}\in g_kSS^{-1}gm​=gk​s′s−1∈gk​SS−1, which contradicts the choice of gmg_mgm​. So the supports are pairwise disjoint.

At each point at most one term of FNF_NFN​ is nonzero, so 0≤FN≤sup⁡f0\le F_N\le\sup f0≤FN​≤supf. Left invariance in Theorem 16.3(c) gives ∫Gfk dLx=∫Gf dLx\int_Gf_k\,d_Lx=\int_Gf\,d_Lx∫G​fk​dL​x=∫G​fdL​x, and this value is positive by the positivity statement (I1). 

So the left Haar integral is unbounded on functions in Cc(G)C_c(G)Cc​(G) with values in [0,sup⁡f][0,\sup f][0,supf], and the total mass of GGG is infinite. The right Haar integral behaves in the same way, with right translates. A noncompact Lie group therefore has no normalised finite Haar integral, and the averaging arguments of Lecture 5 are no longer available in general.

16.3 The modular function

Corollary 16.8.

  1. Every compact Lie group is unimodular.

  2. If GGG is connected, then Δ(exp⁡X)=e−tr⁡ad⁡X\Delta(\exp X)=e^{-\tr\ad X}Δ(expX)=e−tradX. So GGG is unimodular if and only if tr⁡ad⁡X=0\tr\ad X=0tradX=0 for all X∈gX\in\gX∈g. This holds when g\gg is abelian, nilpotent or semisimple.

Proof. (a) Since GGG is compact and Δ\DeltaΔ is continuous, the image Δ(G)\Delta(G)Δ(G) is a compact subgroup of (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞). If t≠1t\ne1t=1 lies in it, then so does the unbounded set {tk:k∈Z}\{t^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}{tk:k∈Z}. So Δ(G)={1}\Delta(G)=\{1\}Δ(G)={1}.

(b) We have Ad⁡(exp⁡X)=ead⁡X\Ad(\exp X)=e^{\ad X}Ad(expX)=eadX (Lecture 2) and det⁡eA=etr⁡A\det e^A=e^{\tr A}deteA=etrA. This gives the formula. If all traces vanish, then Δ=1\Delta=1Δ=1 on exp⁡g\exp\gexpg. This set contains a neighbourhood UUU of eee (Lecture 2). The subgroup HHH generated by UUU is open, since hU⊂HhU\subset HhU⊂H for h∈Hh\in Hh∈H. It is closed, since its complement is a union of open cosets. By connectedness H=GH=GH=G, so Δ≡1\Delta\equiv1Δ≡1. Conversely, Δ≡1\Delta\equiv1Δ≡1 gives e−ttr⁡ad⁡X=1e^{-t\tr\ad X}=1e−ttradX=1 for all ttt, so tr⁡ad⁡X=0\tr\ad X=0tradX=0. For nilpotent g\gg each ad⁡X\ad XadX is nilpotent. For semisimple g\gg we have g=[g,g]\g=[\g,\g]g=[g,g] and tr⁡ad⁡[X,Y]=tr⁡[ad⁡X,ad⁡Y]=0\tr\ad[X,Y]=\tr[\ad X,\ad Y]=0trad[X,Y]=tr[adX,adY]=0.

16.6 Locally compact groups

A topological group is locally compact if eee has a compact neighbourhood. We cite the following result (Folland, A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis, Chapter 2). Let GGG be a locally compact Hausdorff group. A linear functional III on Cc(G)C_c(G)Cc​(G) is positive if I(f)≥0I(f)\ge0I(f)≥0 whenever f≥0f\ge0f≥0. There is a nonzero positive linear functional III on Cc(G)C_c(G)Cc​(G) with I(f(g ⋅))=I(f)I(f(g\,\cdot))=I(f)I(f(g⋅))=I(f) for all f∈Cc(G)f\in C_c(G)f∈Cc​(G) and g∈Gg\in Gg∈G. It is unique up to a positive factor. There is a unique continuous homomorphism Δ ⁣:G→(0,∞)\Delta\colon G\to(0,\infty)Δ:G→(0,∞) satisfying I(f(⋅ g−1))=Δ(g)I(f)I(f(\cdot\,g^{-1}))=\Delta(g)I(f)I(f(⋅g−1))=Δ(g)I(f).

A general locally compact group has no normalisation at eee that compares left and right integrals. The cited result instead contains two identities. They replace the density relation in Theorem 16.6(ii) and the inversion identities in part (iii). First, the functional f↦I(fΔ−1)f\mapsto I(f\Delta^{-1})f↦I(fΔ−1) is right-invariant. Second, III takes the same value on f∈Cc(G)f\in C_c(G)f∈Cc​(G) and on the function x↦f(x−1)Δ(x−1)x\mapsto f(x^{-1})\Delta(x^{-1})x↦f(x−1)Δ(x−1).

The Riesz representation theorem realises III as a Radon measure. We cite Folland, Real Analysis, second edition, Theorem 7.2 in §7.1.

For a Lie group, uniqueness makes III a multiple of f↦∫Gf dLxf\mapsto\int_Gf\,d_Lxf↦∫G​fdL​x. So the two modular functions agree. Since Cc(G)C_c(G)Cc​(G) is dense in L2L^2L2 of a Radon measure (Folland, Real Analysis, Proposition 7.9 in §7.2), our L2(G)L^2(G)L2(G) is the usual one, in the sense made precise below.

Integration rules for Part II

We now collect the measure theory used in the rest of Part II. We cite it from Folland, Real Analysis, second edition, Chapters 2, 6 and 7, and we do not prove it. Let XXX be a Lie group, a quotient G/HG/HG/H of a Lie group by a closed subgroup, or an open subset of Rn\R^nRn. Such a space is locally compact and second countable, and it is a countable union of compact sets. We state the rules only for these spaces. General locally compact groups need further hypotheses in the product theorems.

A Borel set of XXX is a member of the σ\sigmaσ-algebra generated by the open sets. A function f ⁣:X→Cf\colon X\to\Cf:X→C is measurable if the preimage of every open set is a Borel set. A positive Radon measure μ\muμ on XXX assigns a value in [0,∞][0,\infty][0,∞] to each Borel set. It is countably additive and finite on compact sets. On our spaces μ(E)\mu(E)μ(E) is the infimum of μ(U)\mu(U)μ(U) over open U⊃EU\supset EU⊃E, and the supremum of μ(K)\mu(K)μ(K) over compact K⊂EK\subset EK⊂E. A null set is a Borel set of measure 000, or a subset of one. A property holds almost everywhere if it fails only on a null set.

The word “positive” says only that the values are nonnegative. The measure μ\muμ has full support if μ(U)>0\mu(U)>0μ(U)>0 for every nonempty open set UUU. Equivalently, ∫Xφ dμ>0\int_X\varphi\,d\mu>0∫X​φdμ>0 for every nonzero φ∈Cc(X)\varphi\in C_c(X)φ∈Cc​(X) with φ≥0\varphi\ge0φ≥0. For example, the point mass at eee is a positive Radon measure without full support. Haar measures have full support by the positivity statement (I1), and so do the quotient measures of Lecture 17. Lecture 25 also uses positive measures without full support.

Suppose that μ\muμ has full support. Then ∫Xφˉψ dμ\int_X\bar\varphi\psi\,d\mu∫X​φˉ​ψdμ is an inner product on Cc(X)C_c(X)Cc​(X), and its Hilbert completion is the usual space L2(X,μ)L^2(X,\mu)L2(X,μ). Its vectors are the measurable fff with ∫X∣f∣2 dμ<∞\int_X|f|^2\,d\mu<\infty∫X​∣f∣2dμ<∞, and two functions define one vector when they agree almost everywhere. On R\RR, the elements of the completion L2(R)L^2(\R)L2(R) of Lecture 15 are therefore classes of functions of this kind.

A measurable fff is integrable if ∫X∣f∣ dμ<∞\int_X|f|\,d\mu<\infty∫X​∣f∣dμ<∞. Let μ\muμ and ν\nuν be positive Radon measures on such spaces XXX and YYY. We use the following rules.

  • Tonelli. If F ⁣:X×Y→[0,∞]F\colon X\times Y\to[0,\infty]F:X×Y→[0,∞] is measurable, then the two iterated integrals of FFF are equal. Their common value may be infinite.

  • Fubini. If F ⁣:X×Y→CF\colon X\times Y\to\CF:X×Y→C is measurable and one iterated integral of ∣F∣|F|∣F∣ is finite, then the two iterated integrals of FFF exist, are finite and are equal. We use Tonelli to check the hypothesis.

  • Dominated convergence. Let fjf_jfj​ be measurable with fj→ff_j\to ffj​→f almost everywhere. Suppose there is one integrable function ggg with ∣fj∣≤g|f_j|\le g∣fj​∣≤g almost everywhere for all jjj. Then fff is integrable and ∫Xfj dμ→∫Xf dμ\int_Xf_j\,d\mu\to\int_Xf\,d\mu∫X​fj​dμ→∫X​fdμ.

  • Differentiation under the integral. Let I⊂RI\subset\RI⊂R be an open interval. Let F(s,⋅)F(s,\cdot)F(s,⋅) be integrable for each s∈Is\in Is∈I, and let s↦F(s,x)s\mapsto F(s,x)s↦F(s,x) be differentiable for each x∈Xx\in Xx∈X. Suppose there is one integrable function ggg with ∣∂sF(s,x)∣≤g(x)|\partial_sF(s,x)|\le g(x)∣∂s​F(s,x)∣≤g(x) for all s∈Is\in Is∈I and x∈Xx\in Xx∈X. Then dds∫XF(s,x) dμ(x)=∫X∂sF(s,x) dμ(x)\frac{d}{ds}\int_XF(s,x)\,d\mu(x)=\int_X\partial_sF(s,x)\,d\mu(x)dsd​∫X​F(s,x)dμ(x)=∫X​∂s​F(s,x)dμ(x). Indeed, the mean value inequality bounds the difference quotients by ggg, and dominated convergence applies to them.

  • Change of variables. Let Φ ⁣:U→V\Phi\colon U\to VΦ:U→V be a C1C^1C1 diffeomorphism of open subsets of Rn\R^nRn, and let f ⁣:V→Cf\colon V\to\Cf:V→C be integrable, or measurable with values in [0,∞][0,\infty][0,∞]. Then ∫Vf(y) dy=∫Uf(Φ(x)) ∣det⁡DΦ(x)∣ dx\int_Vf(y)\,dy=\int_Uf(\Phi(x))\,|\det D\Phi(x)|\,dx∫V​f(y)dy=∫U​f(Φ(x))∣detDΦ(x)∣dx.

The common bound in dominated convergence cannot be dropped. On R\RR the functions j 1(0,1/j)j\,\mathbf1_{(0,1/j)}j1(0,1/j)​ tend to 000 everywhere, but each has integral 111. For the differentiation rule, take F(s,t)=e−t2+istF(s,t)=e^{-t^2+ist}F(s,t)=e−t2+ist on R\RR. Then ∣∂sF(s,t)∣=∣t∣e−t2|\partial_sF(s,t)|=|t|e^{-t^2}∣∂s​F(s,t)∣=∣t∣e−t2, which is integrable and does not depend on sss. So ∫Re−t2+ist dt\int_\R e^{-t^2+ist}\,dt∫R​e−t2+istdt may be differentiated under the integral.

For Tonelli and Fubini, here is the bound that Lecture 18 uses. Let f,h∈L2(R)f,h\in L^2(\R)f,h∈L2(R) and λ≠0\lambda\ne0λ=0. Tonelli lets us integrate over ttt first. Cauchy–Schwarz and translation invariance bound the inner integral by ∥h∥ ∥f∥\|h\|\,\|f\|∥h∥∥f∥. The two Gaussian integrals are 2π2\sqrt\pi2π​ and 2π/∣λ∣2\sqrt\pi/|\lambda|2π​/∣λ∣. Hence ∫R2e−(a2+λ2b2)/4∫R∣h(t)∣ ∣f(t+a)∣ dt da db≤4π∣λ∣ ∥h∥ ∥f∥.\int_{\R^2}e^{-(a^2+\lambda^2b^2)/4}\int_\R|h(t)|\,|f(t+a)|\,dt\,da\,db\le\frac{4\pi}{|\lambda|}\,\|h\|\,\|f\|.∫R2​e−(a2+λ2b2)/4∫R​∣h(t)∣∣f(t+a)∣dtdadb≤∣λ∣4π​∥h∥∥f∥. This finite bound is the hypothesis of Fubini for the same integrand without absolute values.

Self-checks

  1. In the ax+bax+bax+b group let g=g(2,5)g=g(2,5)g=g(2,5). Suppose ∫Gf dLx=7\int_Gf\,d_Lx=7∫G​fdL​x=7. Find Δ(g)\Delta(g)Δ(g) and ∫Gf(xg) dLx\int_Gf(xg)\,d_Lx∫G​f(xg)dL​x.

    Answer. Δ(g)=1/2\Delta(g)=1/2Δ(g)=1/2. By the right-translation identity in Theorem 16.6(i), the integral is Δ(g)−1⋅7=14\Delta(g)^{-1}\cdot7=14Δ(g)−1⋅7=14.

  2. Suppose some left-invariant smooth positive density on GGG is also right-invariant. Must GGG be unimodular?

    Answer. Yes. By the uniqueness in Theorem 16.3(a), the density is cμLc\mu_LcμL​ for some c>0c>0c>0, so Rg∗μL=μLR_g^*\mu_L=\mu_LRg∗​μL​=μL​ for all g∈Gg\in Gg∈G. By the right-translation identity in Theorem 16.6(i), this means Δ(g)=1\Delta(g)=1Δ(g)=1 for all g∈Gg\in Gg∈G.

  3. On the ax+bax+bax+b group, by what factor does f↦f(⋅ g(3,1))f\mapsto f(\cdot\,g(3,1))f↦f(⋅g(3,1)) multiply ∥f∥2\|f\|^2∥f∥2 in L2(G)L^2(G)L2(G)?

    Answer. By the right-translation identity in Theorem 16.6(i), applied to ∣f∣2|f|^2∣f∣2, the factor is Δ(g(3,1))−1=3\Delta(g(3,1))^{-1}=3Δ(g(3,1))−1=3. Hence the map is not unitary without the factor Δ1/2\Delta^{1/2}Δ1/2.

Summary

Translating a fixed positive density on g\gg gives the left and right Haar densities. Each is unique up to a positive factor. On a noncompact Lie group the total mass is infinite, so no normalised finite Haar integral exists. Right translation scales μL\mu_LμL​ by Δ(g)=∣det⁡Ad⁡(g)∣−1\Delta(g)=|\det\Ad(g)|^{-1}Δ(g)=∣detAd(g)∣−1. When μL\mu_LμL​ and μR\mu_RμR​ have the same value at eee, we have μR=Δ−1μL\mu_R=\Delta^{-1}\mu_LμR​=Δ−1μL​, and inversion exchanges μL\mu_LμL​ and μR\mu_RμR​. For the ax+bax+bax+b group, dLx=a−2 da dbd_Lx=a^{-2}\,da\,dbdL​x=a−2dadb, dRx=a−1 da dbd_Rx=a^{-1}\,da\,dbdR​x=a−1dadb and Δ=a−1\Delta=a^{-1}Δ=a−1. The factor Δ1/2\Delta^{1/2}Δ1/2 makes right translation unitary on L2(G)L^2(G)L2(G). Haar measures and quotient measures are positive Radon measures with full support, and the cited integration rules of §16.6 hold in the second-countable spaces of Part II.

The main groups of Part II are unimodular: Rn\R^nRn, the Heisenberg group, SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R), and the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. Their closed subgroups often are not. For example, the upper triangular subgroup of SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) with positive diagonal is an ax+bax+bax+b group (Exercise 20.6). Lecture 17 compares ΔG\Delta_GΔG​ with ΔH\Delta_HΔH​ to build unitary representations.

Reading

  • Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Chapter VIII “Integration”, sections “Differential Forms and Measure Zero” and “Haar Measure for Lie Groups”. Compare its normalisation of the modular function with ours.

  • Kirillov, Elements of the Theory of Representations, §9, from the course reference route. Check its modular-function convention.

  • Folland, A Course in Abstract Harmonic Analysis, Chapter 2, sections “Haar Measure” and “The Modular Function”, for general locally compact groups.
